text.title: Focus Groups: Structure, Moderation, and Analysis Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules for focus groups: the claim classes the method cannot support, sizing the guide against per-participant airtime, silent-first answers and an attribution log against dominance, segmenting to remove power asymmetry, past-behaviour prompts instead of intention questions, and themes that must replicate across groups.

rule.statement: `themes` MUST NOT contain task-success rates, time-on-task, ease-of-use ratings, findability claims or any statement of the form "users can/cannot do X". A focus group measures stated, socially negotiated opinion. Performance questions MUST be routed out — to usability testing for task success, tree testing for findability, analytics for frequency.

rationale.source: Nielsen, "The Use and Misuse of Focus Groups" (IEEE Software / NN/g, 1997)

rule.rationale: Nobody in the room performs the task, so any performance sentence in the report was inferred from talk. What people say they can do and what they do diverge most where the interface is hardest, which is exactly where the study is being cited.

rule.statement: Group size 6-10, session 90-120 minutes, and the `discussion_guide` MUST be sized against airtime: minutes divided by participants gives each person under 10-15 minutes total across the whole session. Cap the guide at roughly 8-10 main prompts with their probes, and record the arithmetic in the artefact.

rationale.source: Krueger & Casey, Focus Groups: A Practical Guide for Applied Research

rule.rationale: An oversized guide is not compressed evenly — the moderator narrows prompts to yes/no to stay on schedule and starts filling silences, so the last third of the guide collects agreement with the moderator rather than opinion. Sizing the guide up front is the only point at which this is fixable.

rule.statement: For each key question the moderator MUST collect individual written answers before any open discussion, and these MUST be stored alongside `session_notes` so pre-discussion and post-discussion positions can be compared.

rationale.source: Nominal group technique (Delbecq & Van de Ven, 1971); Asch conformity experiments

rule.rationale: The first spoken opinion anchors the room and later speakers adjust toward it — Asch showed people will endorse an obviously wrong answer under mild group pressure. Written-first answers capture the distribution before it collapses, and the gap between the two is itself a finding about how contested the topic is.

rule.statement: Every quote in `session_notes` MUST carry a participant id and timestamp, and the artefact MUST report per-participant share of recorded turns. A session where one participant holds more than about 30% of turns, or where any participant holds under about 5%, MUST be flagged `dominated` and its themes marked accordingly.

rationale.source: Krueger & Casey — moderating dominant talkers and drawing out quiet participants

rule.rationale: In a group of eight, two confident speakers routinely produce most of the transcript. Without attribution the analyst counts mentions, and a theme "raised repeatedly" turns out to be one person's view repeated with seven silent witnesses whose silence gets read as agreement.

rule.statement: The `screener` MUST exclude co-attendance by people in a power or commercial relationship (manager with direct reports, client with vendor, teacher with students) and MUST segment on the variable expected to change the opinion — for example current customers separately from churned, novices separately from experts.
rule.rationale: A subordinate will not contradict their manager in the room, so the group returns the manager's position with apparent consensus. Mixing segments produces the other failure: the transcript averages two incompatible mental models into a theme that describes nobody and satisfies no design decision.

rule.statement: Guide prompts MUST be open and anchored to specific past events ("tell me about the last time you had to do X"). Hypothetical, preference and pricing questions ("would you use this", "how much would you pay", "which of these do you prefer") MUST either be excluded or recorded as stated intention and labelled as such — never cited as evidence of demand.

rationale.source: Nielsen, "The Use and Misuse of Focus Groups"; stated-preference vs revealed-preference gap

rule.rationale: Agreeing with a proposed feature is the cheapest and most socially agreeable thing a participant can say, and the group rewards it. Stated future intent predicts actual adoption weakly, so a roadmap built on group enthusiasm ships features whose usage curve nobody in the room ever committed to.

rule.statement: A theme MUST cite quotes from at least two participants; where more than one group ran, a theme appearing in only one group MUST be labelled group-specific. Run at least two groups per segment before any theme is reported as a segment property.

rationale.source: Krueger & Casey — running multiple groups per segment to reach saturation

rule.rationale: Themes are partly a property of the room: an idea voiced early in one session propagates within that session and can dominate its transcript without existing in the population. Replication in an independent group is the only available control for the group's own dynamics.
